To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) tumours consisting of less viscous (i.e. poorly differentiated) cells grow more rapidly than those consisting of more viscous (i. e. well-differentiated) cells, and (2) the growth of tumours is more rapid if the cells are less sensitive to the interphase drag, or if they are mechanically stressed by the extracellular fluid.

the tumour volume fraction and the cell speed evolve in a way that depends on the cellular viscosity, the interphase drag, the cellular tension and the oxygen tension, while the oxygen tension is a function of the tumour volume and cell density.

the growth of a tumour is determined by a competition between two mechanisms, namely cell proliferation and cell death, which is affected by the mechanical stress experienced by the cells, as well as the oxygen tension within the tumour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the modelling of avascular tumour cell growth, with a focus on the role of cell-cell and cell-extracellular interactions.
developing mathematical models to describe the dynamics of avascular tumour cell proliferation.
the role of cell-cell and cell-extracellular matrix interactions on tumour growth and spread.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a model that can be used to study the role of cell-cell and cell-oxygen interactions on avascular tumour development and growth.
cell-cell interaction plays an important role in the growth dynamics of a two-phase model.

the tumour cell population is a viscous fluid, the cells interact with each other through short-range attractive and long-range repulsive forces, the oxygen concentration is low and the cells grow at a rate proportional to the oxygen concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tumour growth rate is a function of the balance between the interplay of cellular viscosity and cell-cell interactions.

the mechanical properties of the cells and their interactions with the surrounding matrix play an important role in the dynamics of tumour growth, and that these effects can only be properly accounted for in a multi-phase model.
the tumour volume fraction and speed are not independent of each other and that both depend on the cellular viscosity.
